name: Nikhil Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of three people at Oakmere Studio in a market town. We do branding for family businesses: a bakery's new logo, a garage's price boards, a farm shop's labels and website. I use AI tools every day, for first drafts, photo fixes and the text on the websites. Martin, the owner, is sixty-one and still sketches on paper, so I'm the tools person.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love sitting in a bakery at seven in the morning hearing the owner talk about her grandmother's recipe, and turning that into a logo. What's hard is that my design eye isn't there yet, and Martin sends a lot back with a red pen. I'm quicker than good, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to work. The tools are handy and I'd keep using them. Small businesses still need someone they trust to make them look good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a decent world for me. I'm quick with the tools, the clients like me, and I've got about five months saved. The only real question is what Martin does when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to get faster and spend my evenings on proper typography, because Martin's red pen is right most of the time. I'd keep saving, maybe two hundred a month. And I'd start asking Martin, carefully, about buying into Oakmere one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Martin is sixty-one. Has he talked about what happens next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's mentioned it twice over lunch, that he'd like to slow down at sixty-five. He hasn't said who'd take over, and I'd like it to be me. I'd rather own a small business than work for a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner Priya do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Priya keeps the books at her family's hardware shop. She's careful with money, more than me, and she thinks buying into Oakmere is a good idea if the numbers make sense. Her dad built that shop from nothing, so she understands small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small firms that move quickly. People should learn the tools instead of asking for protection. I'd say that to anyone, even if it's not popular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a bakery could make its own logo with a tool, and some will. But most of our clients don't have time and don't trust themselves to judge it. If Oakmere becomes the place that does all of it, logo, website, social posts, for one monthly fee, we could do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Martin and pitch a monthly package for family businesses, run mostly with AI tools and checked by us. I'd offer to put five thousand of my savings into the firm for a small share. And I'd spend evenings learning the tools for websites and social posts, not just logos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried. It's a risk, and I'd rather take it than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI takes over design tasks, what is Oakmere actually selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Trust, mostly. A baker doesn't want to learn design software, because a baker wants someone local and trusted to sort it out. We'd be selling time and judgment, not drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Juniors at the big agencies in the city, the ones who only resize ads. And maybe Martin, if he won't change. I'd hate that, he taught me most of what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small businesses need to stick together and keep money local. I'd say people should help each other rather than wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's hard. By 2028, a bakery owner could have an AI do everything we do, and many will. Our only edge is that people still want a face they know, and I don't know if that's worth a monthly fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on putting my savings into Oakmere and keep them as a cushion. I'd turn Oakmere into a service that sets up the AI for family firms and checks it, charging by the year. And I'd look at Priya's family hardware shop, which is hands-on and might need help with its own setup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've always felt one step ahead, and this is the first time I feel like I'm running behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're putting savings into a firm that AI could replace. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with two years, no. That's why I'd hold the money back. Owning a firm is only good if the firm has a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Priya say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say keep the cushion and help at the hardware shop if needed. Her dad's said I could work there, and with robots three years behind, the shop has longer than Oakmere does.

I'd say people should **help each other** before waiting for government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so small firms should change now and not wait to be rescued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, design as Martin knows it ends around 2030. But five years is enough to turn Oakmere into a business that runs AI for family firms and still has a person they trust. If Martin sells to me in 2027, I'd have a few good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a small share of Oakmere this year, carefully, maybe three thousand. I'd set up the monthly AI package and get ten clients on it. And I'd keep two months of savings separate, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's a gamble with a decent chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can buy in, make it work, and get out if I need to. Two years doesn't give me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to own Oakmere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as I can sell or close it in time. I'd keep an eye on the numbers every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. Small businesses that adapt will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be in a good position. I'd buy Oakmere when Martin retires, build the AI service and have years to grow it. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven and owning something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into Oakmere next year and take it over when Martin turns sixty-five. I'd automate the routine work and spend my time with clients. And Priya and I would get married and buy a small house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and excited. It's the version I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound relaxed. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. Ten years is long enough to build something and sell it if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya and I would marry next year and save for a house, and maybe children in a few years. With ten years of warning, I wouldn't put my life on hold.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build anything before the ground moved. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to change, and less red tape, so family businesses can adapt quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about trust. Everyone talks about what AI can do, but the bakery owner doesn't care about that. Every family business owner I know just wants a designer who will still be around next year.

His **free-market views** favour adapting and ownership over protection.
He plans to **buy into** Oakmere when Martin retires.
Two years makes him **hold back**, while ten makes him calm and ambitious.
